prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: defendant officer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Officer is entitled to qualified immunity because no clearly established law forbade tasing an actively resisting suspect.**

Qualified immunity shields officers from civil liability unless (1) they violated a constitutional right that (2) was clearly established at the time of the conduct. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 232 (2009). A right is clearly established only when existing precedent places the constitutional question "beyond debate," *Mullenix v. Luna*, 577 U.S. 7, 12 (2015) (per curiam), and defines the right with specificity rather than "at a high level of generality," *District of Columbia v. Wesby*, 583 U.S. 48, 63 (2018). That requirement is "especially important in the Fourth Amendment context," where the excessive-force inquiry turns on the facts of each encounter. *Mullenix*, 577 U.S. at 12; *Rivas-Villegas v. Cortesluna*, 595 U.S. 1, 5–6 (2021) (per curiam). Plaintiff cannot meet that burden.

**A. Force against an actively resisting suspect is judged under *Graham*, and this Court has repeatedly found taser use reasonable in that setting.**

Reasonableness under *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989), turns on the severity of the crime, the immediate threat to safety, and whether the suspect is actively resisting or fleeing. This Court applies those factors from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene. *Latits v. Phillips*, 878 F.3d 541, 547–48 (6th Cir. 2017). Active resistance weighs heavily for the officer. As this Court has explained, a suspect who is actively resisting arrest cannot be said to be under the officer's control. *Goodwin v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314, 326 (6th Cir. 2015).

This Court has applied that principle to taser use. In *Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638, 641–42 (6th Cir. 2015), it held that an officer who tased a suspect who was resisting arrest and refusing to submit was entitled to qualified immunity, because a taser was a reasonable means of gaining control. In *Hagans v. Franklin County Sheriff's Office*, 695 F.3d 505, 509–10 (6th Cir. 2012), the Court likewise found no constitutional violation where an officer used a taser on a person who refused to comply and resisted. And in *Kent v. Oakland County*, 810 F.3d 384, 391–92 (6th Cir. 2016), it upheld the use of a taser where the plaintiff was actively resisting the officers' efforts to gain control. These decisions confirm that no settled authority prohibits tasing a suspect who is physically resisting.

**B. The cases denying immunity involve suspects who were not resisting.**

Plaintiff will point to decisions in which this Court denied immunity for taser use. Those decisions are distinguishable because the suspects in them were not actively resisting. In *Goodwin*, 781 F.3d at 326–28, the Court held that tasing a suspect who was not resisting, and who had been compliant or incapacitated, could violate clearly established law. In *Grawey v. Drury*, 567 F.3d 302, 314 (6th Cir. 2009), the plaintiff posed no threat and had not resisted when he was tased. And in *Roell v. Hamilton County*, 870 F.3d 471, 488–89 (6th Cir. 2017), the force was used on a person who was already restrained and subdued. Those cases rest on the absence of resistance. They do not give a reasonable officer fair notice that tasing a person who *is* actively resisting is unlawful. If anything, they confirm that resistance is the line separating lawful from unlawful taser use in this Circuit.

**C. Plaintiff cannot identify controlling authority placing the question beyond debate.**

The record shows that Plaintiff was actively resisting when the Officer deployed the taser. Under *Rudlaff*, *Hagans*, and *Kent*, an officer facing that resistance could reasonably believe a taser was a lawful way to gain control. Plaintiff has identified no Supreme Court or published Sixth Circuit decision holding otherwise on comparable facts. Absent such a case, the Officer lacked fair notice, and the district court erred in denying qualified immunity. This Court should reverse.
